## Methods

Materials
Pd(CH3COO)2 (99.9%), polystyrene (PS), and polyurethane (PU) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. 1-Adamantanethiol (Adm-SH, 99%), triphenylphosphine (PPh3), (Ph2P)2CH2 (DPPM), sodium borohydride (NaBH4, 99.8%), triphenylmethanethiol, 2-phenylethanethiol, benzenemethanethiol, cyclohexanethiol, 4-tert-butylphenylthiol, 2,4-dimethylbenzenethiol, toluene, dichloromethane (DCM), tetrahydrofuran (THF), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), and methanol were all purchased from Shanghai Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Pd8‒S nanocluster was prepared according to our previously report15. All chemicals were used as received. The water used in all experiments was ultrapure (resistivity 18.2 MΩ·cm), produced by a Milli-Q NANOpure water system.

Synthesis of Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(S-Adm)6 (denoted as Pd8‒S)15
Pd(CH3COO)2 (50.0 mg, 0.223 mmol) and PPh3 (100.0 mg, 0.381 mmol) were co-dissolved in 8 mL of THF in a three-necked flask with continuous stirring for 5 min, accompanied by a solution color change from yellow to red. Then, a cold water solution containing NaBH4 (100.0 mg, 2.643 mmol) and Adm-SH (150.0 mg, 0.891 mmol) was immediately added all at once under vigorous stirring, accompanied by the solution color turn from red to dark. 25 min later, multi-sized Pd nanoclusters Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z were precipitated out and washed with excess methanol. The Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z nanoclusters were redissolved in toluene (10 mL) and water (5 mL) mixed solution and heated at 80 °C for 24 h. After this two-phase reaction was completed, the black organic solution was washed with methanol for three times. Pd8‒S was isolated from the crude product by preparative thin-layer chromatography (PTLC) in 10.0 mg (yield: 11%, based on the starting material Pd(CH3COO)2). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixture solution of Pd8‒S in DCM/methanol (4:3; 1 mL) for 3 days.

Synthesis of Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(Ph2P=O)(S-Adm)5 (denoted as Pd8‒P)
Pd8‒S (3 mg, 1.16 × 10−3 mmol) and PPh3 (10.0 mg, 0.0381 mmol) were co-dissolved in 2 mL of toluene in a round-bottomed flask with continuous stirring and heated at 80 °C for over 2 weeks under air atmosphere. After the reaction was completed, the black solution was concentrated under reduced pressure to dryness. Pd8‒P was isolated from the crude product of 20 combined reaction batches by preparative thin-layer chromatography (PTLC) in 1.2 mg (yield: 2%, based on the starting material Pd8‒S). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixed solution of Pd8‒P in DCM/methanol (4:3; 1 mL) over 3 days.

Synthesis of Pd6(PPh)(PPh3)(S-Adm)6 (denoted as Pd6)
Pd(CH3COO)2 (50.0 mg, 0.223 mmol) and PPh3 (100.0 mg, 0.381 mmol) were co-dissolved in 8 mL of THF in a three-necked flask with continuous stirring for 5 min, accompanied by a solution color change from yellow to red. Then, a cold water solution containing NaBH4 (100.0 mg, 2.643 mmol) and Adm-SH (150.0 mg, 0.891 mmol) was immediately added all at once under vigorous stirring, accompanied by the solution color turn from red to dark. 10 min later, multi-sized Pd nanoclusters Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z (x, y, and z denote the number of the unit in a nanocluster, and x is larger than z) were precipitated out and washed with excess methanol. The Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z nanoclusters were redissolved in a toluene (10 mL) and water (5 mL) mixed solution and heated at 80 °C for 6 h (This process can turn the muti-sized Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z nanoclusters to narrowly distributed nanoclusters—size-focusing58. The use of a toluene/water mixed solvent can accelerate the size-focusing, possibly due to some hydrophilic byproducts that can migrate to the water phase, thus promoting the reaction. After this two-phase reaction was completed, the black organic solution was washed with methanol three times. Pd6 was isolated from the crude product by PTLC in 22.4 mg (yield: 30%, based on the starting material Pd(CH3COO)2). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixed solution of Pd6 in DCM/methanol (3:5; 1 mL) for 3 days.

Synthesis of Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2O] (denoted as Pd5‒O)
Pd6 (3 mg, 1.49 × 10−3 mmol) and PPh3 (10.0 mg, 0.0381 mmol) were co-dissolved in 2 mL of toluene in a round-bottomed flask with continuous stirring and heated at 60 °C for over 2 weeks under air atmosphere After the reaction was completed, the black solution was concentrated under reduced pressure to dryness. Pd5‒O was isolated from the crude product of 20 combined reaction batches by PTLC in 1.5 mg (yield: 3%, based on the starting material Pd6). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixture solution of Pd5‒O in DCM/methanol (4:3; 1 mL) over 6 days.

Synthesis of Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2CH2] (denoted as Pd5‒C)
Pd(CH3COO)2 (50.0 mg, 0.223 mmol) and DPPM (100.0 mg, 0.260 mmol) were co-dissolved in 8 mL of THF in a three-necked flask with continuous stirring for 5 min, accompanied by a solution color change from yellow to red. Then, a cold water solution containing NaBH4 (100.0 mg, 2.643 mmol) and Adm-SH (150.0 mg, 0.891 mmol) was immediately added all at once under vigorous stirring, accompanied by the solution color turn from red to dark. 30 min later, multi-sized Pd nanoclusters were precipitated out and washed with excess methanol. The precipitate was redissolved in toluene (10 mL) and water (5 mL), mixed solution and heated at 80 °C for 24 h. After this two-phase reaction was completed, the black organic solution was washed with methanol for three times. Pd5‒C was isolated from the crude product by PTLC in 9.8 mg (yield: 13%, based on the starting material Pd(CH3COO)2). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixed solution of Pd5‒C in DCM/methanol (5:4; 1 mL) over 5 days. Pd5‒C nanocluster could also be obtained by the ligand exchange reaction of Pd5‒O (3 mg, 1.77 × 10−3 mmol) and DPPM (10.0 mg, 0.026 mmol) in 2 mL of toluene and heated at 60 °C for 5 h under air atmosphere.

Note that, inverse palladocenes with planar aromatic Pd5 ring unit and unanticipated nonmental-to-metal aromatic Pd5 ring coordination are synthesized under aqueous-, oxygen-containing conditions and demonstrate remarkable stability in air atmosphere, distinctly differing from reported Pd clusters such as cubic Pd8(PAr)6 clusters59, planar Pd7 clusters60 and Pd4 clusters61 (which require strict anhydrous- and oxygen-free conditions for synthesis and most of them are sensitive to air atmosphere).

Construction of Pd nanoclusters/PS and Pd nanoclusters/PU composites
Pd nanoclusters (1 mg) and PS (100 mg) were co-dissolved in 1.5 mL of DCM and dropwise added into quartz grooves. After the volatilization of DCM, pressure was applied to the Pd nanoclusters/PS composites between two quartz sheets, and they were placed under reduced pressure in a vacuum oven for 12 h to fix their shape. To measure the PCE of Pd nanoclusters, the as-prepared Pd nanoclusters/PS films were shaped into 1 cm2 circular discs with a thickness of 0.20‒0.26 mm (detailed calculation procedures are provided in the Photothermal effects and efficiency calculation section of the Supplementary Information). The Pd nanoclusters/PU composites were constructed using a similar process as that for the Pd nanoclusters/PS composites; however, the PU needed to be dissolved in DMF instead of DCM at 90 °C for 12 h.

Characterization
All UV/Vis/NIR absorption spectra were acquired in the wavelength range of 190–1200 nm using a UV-2550 spectrophotometer. Electrospray ionization mass spectra (ESI‒MS) were recorded using a Waters Q-TOF mass spectrometer utilizing a Z-spray source. The sample was first dissolved in toluene (~0.5 g/L) and then diluted (2/1 v/v) with an ethanol solution containing 50 mmol of CsOAc. The sample was directly infused into the chamber at a flow rate of 5 μL/min. The source temperature was maintained at 70 °C, the spray voltage was 2.20 kV, and the cone voltage was adjusted to 60 V. The single crystal X-ray crystallography (SCXC) data of inverse palladocenes were collected using a Bruker D8 VENTURE CMOS PHOTON 100 diffractometer with a Helios MX multilayer monochromator using Ga Kα radiation (λ=1.34139 Å), while the (Ph2P=O) were collected using a XtaLAB Synergy R, HyPix four-circle diffractometer with a mirror monochromator using Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.54184 Å). 1H, 13C, and 31P NMR spectra were recorded with a Bruker Avance-400 spectrometer. The photoluminescence (PL) properties were recorded by a OmniFluo990 LSP using a xenon lamp as the excitation source under liquid nitrogen. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed using a Thermo Scientific K-Alpha XPS spectrometer. Thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA) of Pd nanoclusters (~5 mg) was conducted in a N2 atmosphere (flow rate ~50 mL/min) on a TG/DTA 6300 analyzer (Seiko Instruments, Inc), with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) characterization was carried out on a Hitachi SU8020 under an accelerating voltage of 10 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization was carried out on a Tecnai G2 F20 under the accelerating voltage of 200 kV. Photothermal measurements were conducted using 980 nm (LSR980F-3W-FC), 1064 nm (LSR1064PD-3W-FC), and 1208 nm (LSR1208NL-1.5W-FC) lasers. The temperature was measured using a thermal imager infrared camera (Fotric 227S), with an error range of ±2.0 °C. Real-time temperatures and infrared photos were extracted from the video by FLIR tools software. Laser power was measured by HS1-USB 0516RI24U device with the software of Power Meter-USB. A conventional three-electrode system was used for differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) measurement. The saturated calomel electrode (SCE) (with saturated KCl solution) and carbon rods are used as a reference (RE) and counter electrode (CE), respectively. A Pt disk electrode (1 mm diameter) was used as working electrode (WE). The electrode potentials were controlled by a potentiostat (Zahner, Germen). The inverse palladocenes were dissolved in CH2Cl2/0.1 M Bu4NPF6 of that was constantly purged by N2 (99.99% Nanjing Special Gas Corp.) during the experiments. All electrochemical experiments were carried out at room temperature (ca. 25 °C).

Computational details
The geometry optimizations of the Pd5‒C, Pd5‒O, Pd6, Pd8‒S, and Pd8‒P inverse palladocenes were conducted by using density functional theory (DFT) with the ORCA 4.2.1 package62. The hybrid PBE0 functional and def2-SVP basis sets63,64 were adopted, where all-electron basis sets were used for H, C, P, and S atoms, while relativistic effective core potentials (RECP) with the associated valence basis set were applied for Pd atom. NBO 7.0 package65 was utilized to perform natural population analysis (NPA) and compute natural atomic orbitals (NAOs) for facilitating subsequent adaptive natural density partitioning (AdNDP)66 analyses. AdNDP analysis was calculated with Multiwfn 3.8 package67.

Atomic charge analyses, electron localization functions (ELF)68, and the energy decomposition analysis with natural orbitals for chemical valence (EDA-NOCV)69,70 calculations were performed with Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) functional based on single-point calculations by using ADF 2019.304 package71. The all-electron polarized triple-zeta (TZP) Slater-type basis sets were adopted for Pd atoms, and DZP Slater-type basis sets were adopted for other atoms72. The scalar relativistic (SR) effects were taken into account with the zero-order regular approximation (ZORA)73. Reduced density gradient (RDG)74,75 was calculated with the ORCA 4.2.1 package, in which the RDG curve was visualized by using Multiwfn 3.867 and VMD 1.9.3 software76. The isochemical shielding surfaces (ICSS) analysis was also performed with Multiwfn 3.8 software and visualized by VMD 1.9.3.

The Gibbs free energy calculations at T=298.15 K and P=1 atm were carried out by using PBE77 functional along with LANL2TZ ECP and basis set78,79 for Pd atoms, and all-electron basis set80,81 6–31G* for the rest of atoms. Vibrational frequency calculations were performed to obtain the thermal corrections over the quantum-mechanical energies. Based on the geometries optimized in the gas-phase, single-point calculations were further performed at the higher level of LANL2TZ(f)82 basis set for Pd atoms, and 6–311G*80,81 for the rest of atoms. Dispersion corrections were included in our calculations by employing the D3 version of Grimme’s dispersion with Becke-Johnson damping83. Solvent corrections using the SMD model84 were included by considering the reaction in toluene. All the calculations were performed using the Gaussian 16 package85 unless specified otherwise.

To better reproduce the experimental UV/Vis/NIR absorption spectrum, the simulation was carried out by using the Gaussian 16 package85 with the PBE77 functional for geometry optimization and TD‒DFT calculations. The ECP and basis set LANL2TZ78,79 were used for Pd atoms, and 6–31G* was used for others (H, C, S, and P)80,81. 200 singlet-to-singlet excitation energies were considered in the TD‒DFT calculations. The Kohn‒Sham molecular orbital analysis was performed by using Multiwfn 3.8 program67.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a comprehensive study on the synthesis, characterization, and photothermal properties of a novel
class of Pd-based nanoclusters "inverse palladocenes." The work is highly original and addresses an under-explored area
in organometallic chemistry involving "nonmetal-to-metal" coordination and Pd aromaticity. The inverse palladocenes
demonstrate rigorous structural/electronic characterization and promising applications, particularly in photothermal
conversion and laser shielding.
The study is in general well-organized and the major conclusions are supported by the results, which is suitable for the
audience of Nature Communications. However, there are a few issues should be addressed:
1. In Figure 4f, the RGD plot appears with many jagged edges, making it difficult to fully observe the π-π stacking interaction.
We kindly suggest considering an increase in the number of grid points to improve the visualization.
2. Is there any electron transfer occurring between the phenyl group of the DPPM ligand and the nearby metal five-membered
ring? We kindly suggest calculating the orbital distribution based on the crystal structure to analyze the orbital or
hole-electron distribution within the aggregate. Additionally, it may be helpful to calculate the electrostatic potential of
inverse palladocycles for further analysis.
3. Should the authors provide more details about the testing conditions for the absorption spectra of inverse palladocenes?
For instance, are the samples in the form of powder, thin films, or solutions? If the samples are in solution, it would be
interesting to explore how different polarities of solvents affect their absorption spectra. On the other hand, if the samples are
in the form of powder or thin films, the author could investigate any differences in their absorption spectra under various
conditions.
4. The inverse palladocences synthesized by the author show diverse photothermal conversion capabilities. Referring to the
Jablonski energy level diagram, might a structure with relatively lower photothermal conversion efficiency exhibit
photoluminescence? If this material features near-infrared luminescence properties, its potential application could be greatly
broadened.
5. The author noted that the photothermal conversion originates from the conjugation of the five-membered palladium
aromatic ring of inverse palladocences. However, we also observe five-membered palladium aromatic rings in Pd8 and Pd6.
Why Pd8 and Pd6 don't demonstrate sufficiently strong photothermal conversion capabilities?
6. In the final paragraph of the article, the author mentions that Pd5-C encapsulated in polystyrene assist in the degradation
of polystyrene at 368 °C. However, in supplementary figure 25, the Pd5-C decomposed at ~300 °C and reached a mass loss
of 60% by ~50 °C. Considering this information, why the reaction might specifically occur at 368 °C?
7. It is suggested to present the values involved in the PCE calculation in a table format for better clarity and organization.
8. In which solution was the photothermal conversion tested (Figure 6a), water or toluene?

Response: Thank the reviewer for the comment. Our transition assignments are based
on orbital contributions to excited states, a standard practice in the metal nanocluster
field (see Science 383, 326–330 (2024); Nat. Commun. 15, 7214 (2024); Nat. Chem. 15,
940–947 (2023); J. Am. Chem. Soc. 144, 12381−12389 (2022). etc.).
The metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT)/ligand-to-ligand charge transfer

Question 1: What is the essential difference between Reference 15 (Angew. Chem. Int.
Ed. 63, e202313491 (2024).) and this study?
Response: Thank the reviewer for the question. We did synthesize the
Pd (PPh) (PPh ) (S-Adm) (Pd –S for short) nanocluster previously (Angew. Chem. Int.
8 2 3 2 6 8
Ed. 63, e202313491 (2024)), which might indicate the emergence of a novel type of
material: inverse metallocene. However, we didn’t propose the concept “inverse
metallocene” in that work since additional instances are required to validate a single
case report. In particular, at that time it remained uncertain whether metal five-
membered ring structures analogous to the cyclopentadienyl anion (Cp) structure exist.
Here we proposed the concept “inverse metallocene” and demonstrate that the five-
membered aromatic metal ring is a fundamental metal building block for inverse
metallocene by developing synthesis methods and synthesizing a series of new
compounds. Therefore, one point of this work is that it declares the birth of a novel type
of materials with fundamental study values and great application potentials. There are
some other essential differences between the two works as summarized below:
i) the longest laser irradiation wavelength was extended from the previous 808 nm
to 1208 nm, which is nontrivial for practical applications, and the high
photothermal conversion efficiency (PCE) of 14.7% per metal atom was
achieved in this work, which considerably outperforms that for Pd ‒S and other
8
reported materials as displayed in Fig. 6c and supplementary Table 9;

iii) the application of photothermy was greatly extended to a large range of fields
including laser shielding, high-temperature degradation, ignition and
temperature control in this work, demonstrating great potentials of inverse
palladocenes for practical applications;
iv) the nonmetal-aromatic ring to metallo-aromatic-ring weak interaction was
found in the crystal structure of Pd ‒C, which was not previously reported;

In short, we have made great advances in the synthesis, structure, property and
structure-property correlation study of a novel type of materials, and we have further
expanded the application fields of this type of materials. Therefore, this work is
essentially different from the previous work, and its novelty, significance and impact
are nontrivial.

### Reviewer 1

Whereas I have been initially undecided (if not tentatively supportive) relating to the match between Nat. Commun and this manuscript, the author’s rebuttal has flipped my assessment strongly in disfavor, as many – if not most – of my remarks are not properly addressed despite of the rebuttal’s 21 pages referring to my review. Some of the author's replies are factually incorrect. Overall, the rebuttal casts serious doubts whether the overall manuscript has been composed with appropriate care/honesty to be published in a top-journal:
1.) Being a synthetic chemist, I mentioned that I do not find the synthesis on its own impressive, and that I consider the overall manuscript quite similar to the previous ACIE manuscript, hence limiting to some extent novelty. I understand that others might judge this point differently. Yet, the authors’ reply “this is in strong contrast to the other two reviewers’ comments (see below)” is not ok: None of the other reviewers has assessed the novelty of the underlying synthesis; in fact, reviewer 2 specifically asks: “Question 1: What is the essential difference between Reference 15 (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 63, e202313491 (2024).) and this study?”
2.) The authors correct my statement of “photothermal conversion in the NIR (850 nm)” with “the longest laser irradiation wavelength was extended from the previous 808 (not 850!) nm to 1208 nm”. However, Fig. 3, blue trace in Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 63, e202313491 (2024) clearly indicates that the absorption band is centered way beyond 826 nm. I understand, the authors refer to the laser, yet I was referring to the band… This is not a major issue on its own, yet tentatively suggests that the rebuttal has not been composed with appropriate care and reflection.
3.) I mentioned that the manuscript would benefit from carving out structure (i.e. Pd5/ligand) – property (i.e. PCE properties) relationships. This question was answered with the Sncp, although I mentioned the Sncp only later, i.e. it seems also this part of my assessment was not read carefully and/or ignored…
4.) I questioned the usefulness of Sncp beyond more established descriptors (such as these reviewed/developed by the Sola group). I am still not convinced that it is superior to these descriptors, as the authors just repeated its definition; I am certainly not convinced that it deserves to be specifically highlighted…
5.) I pointed out that the assignment as a simple HOMO-LUMO transition is inappropriate, as the transitions >950 nm (E <1.3 eV) have a very different energy to the computed HOMO/LUMO gap (E = 2.4 eV = 500 nm), almost a factor of 2. The authors replied, this is due to commonly known dependend on the amount of exact exchange, yet it is (of course) due to orbital mixing, i.e. this reply tentatively suggests a general lack of understanding…
6.) I pointed out that simply plotting canonical orbitals / partial charges do not allow to specify overall oxidation states, and that "charge state" is imprecise language. However, I see that the authors still claim “Molecular orbital (MO) analysis verified the charge state of Pd in various inverse palladocenes.” I note massive orbital mixing with the ligand…
7.) The authors claim in the letter that “Pd8(PAr) clusters, planar Pd7 clusters, and Pd4 clusters are sensitive to air atmosphere and require strict anhydrous- and oxygen-free conditions for synthesis. Due to the exceptional stability of the inverse palladocenes, these novel materials provide great potentials for practical applications in common (aqueous-, oxygen-containing) conditions.” This statement is incorrect, the first example is air stable and water-stable in boiling solvent. Generally, I would not consider this oversight a major issue, yet given all the other inaccuracies, this seems troublesome.
8.) I mentioned it would be interesting to also include/mention/compare the P-signal in the XPS analysis (which usually is obtained along the way of the Pd-measurement). This comment has not been addressed; also this is on its own not a major issue, yet again casts doubt about how carefully the rebuttal/manuscript has been composed
9.) The authors added Supplementary Table 8 to underscore the exceling PCE properties. However, I note that this table seems to compare apples with pears (solution vs. film), and that the properties of quite a bit of reference compounds seem still quite similar…

### Reviewer 2

The authors have addressed all my comments. Thus, I'd like to recommend its publication in the present form.

### Reviewer 3

The author has thoroughly addressed all the questions raised by the reviewers and provided clear and detailed responses.
We believe the article is now ready for publication.

### Reviewer 4

The authors did a thorough job in addressing the questions raised by the different reviewers. The manuscript is written well and the complexes have been thorough investigated and analyzed. So the methodology is sound and most claims are supported by experimental findings.
I agree with referee 1 that the current manuscript is an extension to the authors’ previous work reported in Angewandte Chemie. However, the current contribution contains novel aspects and also shows that this seems to be a novel class of compounds for which different derivatives can be prepared. Hence, I would argue that there is enough novelty to argue for Nature Communications.
However, I would request some revisions and changes:
1) The yields are in some cases rather poor. Can the authors please explicitly specify how much material (in mg) was actually isolated in each case. The reported isolated yield is based on which starting material?
2) What happens if the synthesis is actually performed under strictly anaerobic/anahydrous conditions would these materials be then isolate at all?
3) Please be more specific with the comment: “The thiolate type influences the final products due to the space and electronic effects.” This is a rather general comment. What is more important sterics or electronics?
4) Include in the SI the d-electron counts per palladium atom. In their reply to referee 1 the authors state: “Given that Pd has a d10 electron configuration, the d-electron counts of Pd8–S, Pd8–P, Pd6, Pd5‒O, and Pd5–C are concluded to be 70, 70, 64, 44 and 44, respectively, on the basis of the charge state of Pd.” What do the authors mean with the numbers: 70, 70, 64, 44 and 44??
5) Supplementary Figure 2 (b): Replace “=” by proper arrows.
6) Is it reasonable to compare in the TOC contrast the interaction between the Pd5 fragment and an arene fragment to that of Cp5- and an arene ring? Have the authors directly compared these interactions?
7) Figure S32: Can the authors please label/assign the individual redox events? Some of them seem to be not very reversible.
8) One issue I have with the current manuscript is the authors’ insistence on classifying the metal atom in a classic metallocene complex as electron acceptor, but there is a also delta-backdonation from the metal to the empty orbitals of the Cp- or arene ring. This interaction is completely ignored in the interest of stressing differences. From the bonding analysis I would argue that these systems as the “classic” d-transition metal metallocenes share the feature of strongly covalent covalent molecules.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.

  major_revision

Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

Metallocene research has influenced the development of organometallic chemistry, and the metal–nonmetal inverted half-sandwich structure (inverse metallocene) was very recently discovered. However, additional instances are required to propose the concept inverse metallocene and it remains uncertain whether metal five-membered ring structures analogous to the cyclopentadienyl anion structure exist. Herein we report the synthesis of a series of palladium analogs Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(Ph2P=O)(S-Adm)5 (Pd8–P), Pd6(PPh)(PPh3)(S-Adm)6 (Pd6), Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2O] (Pd5–O), and Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2CH2] (Pd5–C), identify their fundamental metal building block named five-membered Pd aromatic ring, and reveal their conjugation‒photothermy correlation. In particular, we report an average NIR-II photothermal conversion efficiency per metal atom of 14.7% and the stability of the five-membered Pd aromatic ring, as illustrated by the fact that Pd5–C maintained photothermy performance for >10 heating–cooling cycles even after the ligands were removed. We further demonstrate the great potential of inverse palladocenes in areas such as laser shielding, high-temperature degradation, ignition, and temperature/light control. These results declare the research and application start of a type of materials named inverse palladocenes.

---

## Introduction

The isolation and structural elucidation of ferrocene marked the inception of contemporary organometallic chemistry1–4. Since this milestone discovery, sandwich (or half-sandwich) metallocenes have been extensively reported5–8. The cyclopentadienyl anion (Cp, [C5H5]−) serves as the fundamental building block for this type of material. It comprises 6π electrons, adhering to the Hückel 4n+2 rule of aromaticity (Fig. 1a), and giving metallocenes unusual stability for practical applications in biology, pharmaceuticals, materials, etc9–14. However, the extension of this nonmetallic Cp to analogous metal five-membered rings, as well as the prospective metal aromaticity of the latter, requires further investigation. Interestingly, we recently produced an inverse metallocene-like structure15, in which the pentalene (C8H4) anion was replaced by a structurally similar two-fused and conjugated five-membered palladium (Pd5) ring, and the metal cation in metallocene was replaced by a nonmetal anion, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. The revealed nonmetal-to-metal ring coordination, as well as the aromatic Pd8 cation, was not previously reported16–19, which might indicate the emergence of a type of material: inverse metallocene. However, additional instances are required to validate a single case report. Specifically, it remains uncertain whether metal five-membered ring structures analogous to the Cp structure exist, which inspired this work.

Herein, we synthesized a series of inverse metallocene Pd nanoclusters, including Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(Ph2P=O)(S-Adm)5 (Pd8–P for short), Pd6(PPh)(PPh3)(S-Adm)6 (Pd6 for short), Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2O] (Pd5–O for short), and Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2CH2] (Pd5–C for short), as well as the previously reported Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(S-Adm)6 (Pd8–S for short). All of the nanoclusters comprised the Pd5 five-membered aromatic ring unit, demonstrating that Pd8–S is not the only example of an inverse metallocene material and that the five-membered aromatic metal ring is a fundamental metal building block for inverse metallocene (Fig. 1b). Moreover, nonmetal-aromatic ring to metallo-aromatic-ring π…π-like interactions were observed in the Pd5–C nanocluster20–30, indicating the border vagueness of metal and nonmetal aromatic rings. The five-membered aromatic Pd ring gave the series of inverse metallocene stability and ultrahigh NIR-II photothermal conversion efficiency (PCE). In addition, it was revealed that the photothermy was conjugation-related, and the smallest Pd5–C exhibited the highest NIR-II PCE up to 73.6% (irradiated at 980 nm) with an average PCE of 14.7% per Pd atom, which is much higher than that of previously reported photothermy materials31–35. The applications of Pd5–C in laser shielding, high-temperature degradation, ignition, and temperature/light control were also illustrated. The details are shown below.

---

## Results

Synthesis of inverse palladocenes
Initially, we focused on the kinetics tuning of Pd8–S nanocluster synthesis to obtain inverse palladocenes featuring only a single five-membered metal ring unit (Supplementary Fig. 2). Unfortunately, our efforts resulted in the unexpected synthesis of Pd6 nanocluster, which was recently obtained by some other group36 according to the synthesis method of Pd8–S15 (the cited study focused on semihydrogenation catalysis, rather than chemical bonding). We then broke the Pd‒Pd bonds of the Pd8–S and Pd6 nanoclusters to obtain the target inverse palladocene (Supplementary Fig. 2). After 2 weeks of heating at 80 °C, the Pd8–S nanocluster remained unchanged except for a thiolate exchange with a [Ph2P=O]− group (from Ph3P oxidation), forming the Pd8–P nanocluster (Supplementary Fig. 3). In the case of the Pd6 nanocluster, two Pd‒Pd bonds in its three-membered ring were successfully cleaved with the two left triangular vertex Pd atoms protected by a bidentate (Ph2P)2O ligand, leading to the formation of Pd5‒O nanocluster (Supplementary Fig. 4). Note that, Pd5‒O can also be synthesized by a metal salt reduction method with relatively high yield via using Ph2PH(=O) and Ph2PCl as (Ph2P)2O ligand precursors (for detailed procedures, see Metal salt reduction method for the synthesis of Pd5‒O section of the Supplementary Information). Considering the presence of the protective (Ph2P)2O ligand (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 4) in the Pd5‒O nanocluster, we referred the synthesis of Pd8–S, but replacing PPh3 with the bisphosphine (Ph2P)2CH2 (DPPM) ligand, and fortunately achieved the direct synthesis of bisphosphine ligand-protected Pd5‒C nanocluster (see “Methods” for detailed synthesis). The thiolate type influences the final products due to the space and electronic effects, which influence the formation kinetics and thermodynamics of the products37. In our case, the space effect looks more prominent than the electronic effect since only very bulky 1-adamantanethiol led to the production of Pd5–C among the investigated thiolates. For the other thiols (including those with close electronic effects), they led to Pd nanoparticles or complexes as shown in the Supplementary Fig. 5. The synthesis routes for Pd8–P, Pd6, Pd5‒O, and Pd5‒C are illustrated in Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2, and plausible generation pathways for Pd8–P, Pd5‒O, and Pd5‒C are proposed in Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4. Moreover, density functional theory (DFT) calculations indicated that the Gibbs free energies for the transformations from Pd6 to Pd5‒O (and to Pd5‒C) (Fig. 2b) and from Pd8‒S to Pd8–P (Supplementary Fig. 6) were notably negative, demonstrating the transformation thermodynamic favorability.

Characterization of inverse palladocenes
The molecular compositions of the Pd8–P, Pd6, Pd5‒O, and Pd5‒C nanoclusters were all identified using electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI‒MS), as shown in Fig. 2c‒f, and subsequently corroborated by single-crystal X-ray crystallography (SCXC). Specifically, one dominant ion peak at m/z 2763.02 was readily assigned to [Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(Ph2P=O)(S-Adm)5Cs]+ (Fig. 2c; to assist ionization, cesium acetate was added to the nanocluster solution to form [cluster + ×Cs]×+ adducts before ESI‒MS analysis). The isotopic patterns, depicted in the inset of Fig. 2c, supported this assignment with a negligible deviation of 0.17 M/Z between experimental and theoretical values. This finding clearly illustrates that the transformation from Pd8–S to Pd8–P involved the substitution of one [S-Adm]− ligand in Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(S-Adm)6 with one [Ph2P=O]− group (see Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 7 for ESI‒MS comparison). ESI‒MS analysis also revealed the composition of the Pd6 nanocluster (Fig. 2d), with the predominant peak at m/z 2145.71 assigned to [Pd6(PPh)(PPh3)(S-Adm)6Cs]+. Similarly, the ion peaks of Pd5‒O and Pd5–C were attributed to {Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2O]Cs}+ and {Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2CH2]Cs}+, respectively. These assignments were also confirmed by comparing the isotopic patterns of the experimental and calculated results, as shown in the insets of Fig. 2d‒f. The number of Cs+ in these formulas corresponded precisely to the ion charge numbers, affirming the neutrality of the as-obtained species, which was further substantiated by the absence of any rational signal in the mass spectra when Cs+ was not added. Thus, the formulas of the resultant Pd nanoclusters were deduced to be Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(Ph2P=O)(S-Adm)5, Pd6(PPh)(PPh3)(S-Adm)6, Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2O], and Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2CH2].

Given the exact compositions and the recognized formal oxidation states (OSs) of ligands [S-Adm]−, [PPh]2−, [Ph2P=O]−, and PPh3 (–1, –2, –1, and 0, respectively; note: the detailed analysis of the OS of phosphorus in inverse palladocenes is provided in the Analysis of the OS of phosphorus in inverse palladocenes section of the Supplementary Information)15,38, the average OSs of Pd in Pd8–P, Pd6, Pd5‒O, and Pd5–C were calculated to be +1.25, +1.33, +1.2, and +1.2, respectively, indicating the low OSs of Pd across all these nanoclusters39. Molecular orbital (MO) analysis verified the OSs of Pd in various inverse palladocenes. Taking Pd5–C as an example, the revealed three empty MOs is consistent with the total OS of its five Pd atoms (+6) (Supplementary Fig. 8). The low OSs of Pd were further authenticated using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and natural population analysis (NPA) charge, as shown in Fig. 2g‒j and Supplementary Figs. 9‒12.

Geometric and electronic stuctures
SCXC definitively ascertained the compositions of the four Pd nanoclusters (Pd8–P, Pd6, Pd5‒O, and Pd5‒C) and revealed their structures, which were also well reproduced by DFT geometry optimization as shown in Supplementary Table 1, demonstrating the reliability of both the theoretical simulations and experimental results. As mentioned above, Pd8–S and Pd8–P differed solely in one ligand: [S-Adm]− versus [Ph2P=O]−. Pd8–P comprised two pseudo-coplanar metallic pentagon units interconnected by two shared Pd atoms, which was the same as that of Pd8–S15. In contrast, Pd5‒O, Pd5‒C, and Pd6 each fearured a single metallic pentagon unit (Fig. 3a). Among them, Pd5‒C distinguished itself from Pd5‒O by the substitution of the O atom in the bidentate phosphine of Pd5‒O with a CH2 unit. Pd6 incorporated an additional triangular unit alongside its coplanar metallic pentagon unit by sharing two Pd atoms. Overall, these nanoclusters demonstrate the metallic pentagon unit as the fundamental metal building block. The average Pd‒Pd distance within the metallic pentagon units remained consistent at 2.66 Å for Pd8–P, Pd5‒O, and Pd5‒C, consistent with the reported measurement for Pd8–S15. In contrast, Pd6 exhibited a longer mean Pd‒Pd distance of 2.70 Å (Fig. 3b), which can be explained as follows. The triangular unit in Pd6 had an average Pd‒Pd distance of 2.99 Å (Fig. 3c), surpassing that of the metallic pentagon unit and elongating the shared Pd‒Pd bond to 3.05 Å (Fig. 3a). Thus, the metallic pentagon unit in Pd6 had a longer average Pd‒Pd distance than that in Pd8–S, Pd8–P, Pd5‒O, and Pd5‒C nanoclusters. Meticulous inspection revealed that the five Pd atoms in all pentagon units deviated slightly from perfect coplanarity, and the deflection angles for noncoplanar atoms in Pd8–P, Pd8–S, Pd6, Pd5‒O, and Pd5‒C were 37°+35°, 35°+32°, 6°, 3°, and 1°, respectively (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 13), indicating the variation in five-membered ring conjugations. The conjugation disparity was also reflected in the bond length homogenization (Fig. 3a, e). To quantitatively assess this, a concept of nominal coplanar bond length standard deviation (Sncp) was introduced40,41, based on the coplanar five-membered ring formed after the projection of noncoplanar Pd atom(s) (see Supplementary Table 2 for the details). The Sncp values followed the sequence: Pd5‒C (0.078) < Pd5‒O (0.080) < Pd6 (0.201) < Pd8‒S (0.266) < Pd8–P (0.333), positively correlating with the deflection angles. The bond length homogenization and the deflection angle of noncoplanar atoms served as two pivotal physical parameters for evaluating the ring conjugation degree. In addition, the alignment between the sequence of deflection angles and that of nominal coplanar Pd–Pd bond length standard deviations corroborated the hierarchy of the conjugation degree order of Pd5‒C > Pd5‒O > Pd6 > Pd8‒S > Pd8–P (from largest to smallest). These are understandable given the differences in the protecting ligands or fused rings for the conjugated five-membered rings. For instance, in the comparison between Pd5‒C and Pd5‒O, the conjugation degree of the five-membered ring was lower in Pd5‒O than in Pd5‒C owing to the stronger electron-withdrawing capability of O compared to C42,43. Besides, the fused three- or five-membered ring exerts a dampening effect on conjugation, explaining why the conjugation degree of the five-membered ring of Pd5‒O was higher than that of Pd8–S or Pd8–P. The conjugation degree holds substantial implications for numerous physicochemical properties, which will be illustrated below.

Furthermore, DFT calculations were performed for the inverse palladocenes to provide insights into their electronic structure (Fig. 4). The electron localization functions (ELF) map, which provides the probability of finding electron pairs in a given region, suggested that the electrons were evenly distributed between each Pd−Pd pair in the five-, six-, and eight-membered ring units of all these compounds (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 14). Moreover, the theoretical calculations reveal that the five-membered ring in Pd5‒C is aromatic and is the basic unit of these systems (Fig. 4a). As supported by the adaptive natural density partitioning (AdNDP) method, all the Pd5 units have three 6c–2e AdNDP orbitals (Fig. 4b for Pd5‒C, Supplementary Fig. 15 for Pd5‒O, Pd6, Pd8–P, and refer to our previous work15 for Pd8–S), which agree with the 4n+2 rule in the five-membered aromatic ring (Cp and its analogues). Unlike classic d-transition metal metallocenes, wherein the interaction between Cp (or its analogues) and the metal atom involves strong covalent bonding with both Cp (and its analogues)-to-metal atom electron donation and metal atom-to-empty orbitals of Cp (and its analogues) δ-backdonation, inverse palladocenes have major orbital interactions comprising of ligand-to-metal atom coordination, where the Pd5 aromatic ring served as electron acceptor (Supplementary Fig. 16a; the energy decomposition analysis with natural orbitals for chemical valence (EDA-NOCV) of both metallocenes and inverse palladocenes are provided in the EDA-NOCV analysis of inverse palladocenes section of the Supplementary Information). Recently, Sun et al. synthesized two anionic clusters, [Cr5Sn20Sb2]4− and [(Cr)5Sn52Sb6]6−, both of which featured metal aromaticity in the chromium (Cr) segments within their cluster cores without connecting nonmetal atoms (Supplementary Fig. 16b)44. Dehnen et al. isolated a planar π-aromatic Bi5− ring with electron donating nature analogous to the Cp in contrast to our case (Supplementary Fig. 16c)45. The corresponding AdNDP orbital shapes and compositions revealed that Pd5 units featured unique nonmetal-to-metallo-aromatic-ring coordination arising from the orbital interactions between the centroid phosphorus (P) atom and the five adjacent Pd atoms. The aromatic properties of these systems were further supported by the isochemical shielding surface (ICSS), where the simulated [Pd5]6+ (all ligands were removed) and [Pd5(S-Adm)4(DPPM)]2+ (the [PPh]2‒ unit was removed) are analogous to the cases of aromatic [C5H5]‒ (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 17). Furthermore, the ICSSs of the total structural Pd5‒C, Pd5‒O, Pd6, Pd8‒P, and Pd8‒S are also in accordance with the characteristics of aromatic [C5H5]‒ or [C8H6]2‒, as shown in Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 18. The series of compounds not only show environmental stability (water- and oxygen-resistant during the synthesis and use), but also exhibit rather thermostability and photostability (Supplementary Figs. 19 and 20), providing experimental support for their aromaticity.

An intriguing finding in the crystal structure was that one phenyl (Ph) motif of the DPPM ligand in the Pd5‒C was pseudo-parallel to the metallic pentagon unit of the adjacent Pd5‒C (face to face), separated by an inter-ring distance of 3.7 Å. This is formally similar to π…π stacking between organic aromatic rings (e.g., between Ph and Cp), indicating possible π…π-like interactions36 (Fig. 4a, e). Reduced density gradient (RDG) calculations revealed that the similar major van der Waals (vdW) interaction between Ph and Pd5 ring (Fig. 4f), and between Ph and Cp46 (Supplementary Fig. 21). These interactions were also corroborated by independent gradient model based on Hirshfeld partition (IGMH) analysis (Supplementary Fig. 22), which previously disclosed the unreported nonmetal-aromatic ring to metallo-aromatic-ring interactions23,47–51. Taken together, these results demonstrated that the metal-aromatic ring was comparable to the nonmetal-aromatic ring. Energy decomposition analysis (EDA) calculation on a simplified (Pd5‒C)2 dimer based on the crystal structure (Supplementary Table 3), reveals that electrostatic attraction between the phenyl group of the DPPM ligand and the adjacent metal five-membered ring dominates over orbital interactions induced by the electron transfer (accounting for 69.7% vs. 30.3%), which is further confirmed by the electrostatic potential distribution within the dimer. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 23, the plot of electrostatic potential surfaces suggests that the electrostatic potential is asymmetrically distributed among the Pd5‒C: the palladium five-membered ring is more negatively charged while the phenyl group of the DPPM ligand is relatively positive, facilitating their electrostatic attraction between the two moieties. The electrostatic attraction not only oriented all S-Adm ligands codirectional to the [PPh]2− ligands but also resulted in the one-dimensional self-assembly of Pd5‒C into an inverse palladocene supermolecule structure (Fig. 4e). Notably, this assembly adopted an orientation antipodal to that of the neighboring assemblies within the crystal lattice (Fig. 4g). However, such nonmetal-aromatic ring to metallo-aromatic-ring π…π-like interactions were absent in Pd5‒O, with all metallic pentagons in the lattice aligning parallel (Supplementary Fig. 24). This probably arose from intermolecular dense-packing induced by polarity, demonstrating that one atom difference in the ligand of inverse palladocene had a major effect on the intermolecular interactions (Supplementary Fig. 25). The intermolecular interactions considerably influenced the crystallographic arrangement, leading to the 2H arrangements of Pd8‒P and Pd5‒O, and the 4H arrangements of Pd5‒C and Pd6 (Fig. 3f).

Optical and electronic properties
The electronic structures of inverse palladocenes were experimentally investigated using ultraviolet/visible/near infrared (UV/Vis/NIR) spectrometry (Supplementary Figs. 26–29) and further explained by time-dependent (TD)‒DFT calculations (with PBE functional), as shown in Fig. 5 and Supplementary Figs. 30‒32. All of the nanoclusters exhibited NIR absorption characteristics. Specifically, Pd5‒C and Pd5‒O played intense experimental absorption bands within the wavelength window of ~850 to 1150 nm, peaking at 973 and 940 nm, respectively (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 27). Note that the absorptions of inverse palladocenes are solvent dependent. However, not only absorption intensities but also absorption maximum wavelengths don’t positively correlate with the solvent polarity as shown in Supplementary Fig. 29. Kohn‒Sham MO analysis revealed that the predominant contribution (96%) to the simulated Pd5‒C peak at 1050 nm originated from the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) → the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) electronic transitions (Fig. 5b). This was similar to the calculated results of Pd5‒O, in which HOMO→LUMO electronic transitions accounted for the dominant contribution (94%) of the simulated peak at 1010 nm (Supplementary Fig. 30). In contrast, unlike their Pd5‒C and Pd5‒O counterparts, the NIR absorption peaks of Pd6 and Pd8‒P conspicuously blue-shifted into the NIR-I region (Supplementary Figs. 31 and 32). This shift was attributed to structural variations, particularly the presence of fused three-(Pd6) or five-(Pd8‒P) membered ring that reduce the aromaticity of the five-membered Pd ring, which is a common rule observed in organic conjugated systems52–54. The simulated Pd6 peak at 889 nm primarily (90%) arose from HOMO→LUMO electronic transitions, whereas the simulated Pd8‒P peak at 901 nm was attributed to both HOMO→LUMO electronic transitions (accounting for 40%) and HOMO-1→LUMO electronic transitions (accounting for 45%). Using Pd5‒C and Pd5‒O as examples, further disassembling along three axial directions by DFT calculations revealed that the y-axis transition of a metallic pentagon mainly contributed the lowest energy transition (α) (Fig. 5c, d and Supplementary Fig. 30c, d), reflecting in that the transition dipole moment ratios of x, y, and z (x:y:z) were 0.95:2.27:0.04 and 0.29:2.51:0.14 for Pd5‒C and Pd5‒O, respectively (Supplementary Table 4). The HOMO-LUMO gap of 1.09 eV matches well with the optical gap of Pd5‒C (1.18 eV) (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Figs. 27 and 33), which is consistent with the measured electrochemical gap of 1.60 V (Supplementary Fig. 34). Of note, the series of inverse palladocenes have close DPV profiles and electrochemical gaps with 1.63, 1.69, 1.59, and 1.68 V for Pd5‒O, Pd6, Pd8‒S, and Pd8‒P, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 34), providing further support for the existence of metal building block—five-membered aromatic metal ring, which plays the functional group-like55 role.

Photothermal properties
It is documented that dominant longitudinal transitions in metal nanorods56 or x-direction transitions in flat nanoclusters can result in strong photothermal effects15; however, it is unclear if such a major transition along the y-direction could also induce a notable photothermal conversion. Figure 6a shows that under 0.5 W/cm² laser irradiation, 80 μg/mL solutions of Pd5‒C or Pd5‒O exhibited a substantial temperature rise at 980 nm (which wavelength is close to the maximum NIR absorption wavelengths for the five inverse palladocenes: Pd5‒C, Pd5‒O, Pd6, Pd8‒S, and Pd8‒P), achieving PCEs of 73.6% and 68.1%, respectively (see Supplementary Information for detailed calculations). These values surpassed previously reported for nanoclusters and most other photothermal materials under identical irradiation wavelengths (Fig. 6b and Supplementary Table 9). For comparison, the PCEs of the remaining inverse palladocenes (Pd6, Pd8‒S, and Pd8‒P) were also investigated, revealing values of 51.8%, 24.1%, and 20.3%, respectively. Consequently, the PCE rankings among the five inverse palladocenes were Pd5‒C > Pd5‒O > Pd6 > Pd8‒S > Pd8‒P, which intriguingly mirrored their conjugation degree order, indicating the conjugation‒photothermy correlation and that the major photothermy was contributed from the five-membered Pd aromatic ring of inverse palladocenes. Specifically, Pd5 aromatic ring is the primary contributor of the NIR absorption, and thus strong conjugation within the Pd5 ring leads to intensive NIR absorption, enabling enhanced photothermal conversion in the NIR-II window.

To further verify the hypothesis that the five-membered Pd aromatic ring is the major photothermy contributor, we carried out a charge difference density analysis of Pd5‒C during its transition from the ground state to the excited state as shown in Supplementary Fig. 35. The analysis reveals that during the excitation process, electron transfer mainly occurs within the metallic Pd5 aromatic ring and partially involves those between Pd and the [SCH3]‒ ligands. We then computationally simulated the absorption spectrum of Pd5‒C by substituting the [SCH3]‒ ligand with F‒, Cl‒, Br‒, [OCH3]‒, or [SeCH3]‒ groups (Supplementary Fig. 36), which revealed the negligible change in the NIR peak, demonstrating the unessential influence of ligands on the electronic transition associated with the NIR absorption. Moreover, the unchanged photothermy performance for 10 heating–cooling cycles after ligand removal (Supplementary Figs. 37 and 38) served as a compelling evidence that the photothermy of Pd5‒C was dominated by the five-membered Pd aromatic ring. This finding demonstrates that merely five Pd atoms can achieve a remarkable 73.6% of light to heat conversion efficiency, suggesting an average of 14.7% per metal atom, which considerably outperforms that for other reported materials (Fig. 6c and Supplementary Table 10), demonstrating the uniqueness of the five-membered Pd aromatic ring. Notably, although the concentration only slightly affected PCE, it had considerable effect on the temperature rise. For instance, halving the Pd5‒C concentration to 40 μg/mL resulted in a temperature rise of 42.9 °C, whereas increasing it to 200 μg/mL increased the temperature to 65.4 °C (Fig. 6d; for the time-dependent temperature changes, see Fig. 6e and Supplementary Fig. 39). The Pd5‒C inverse palladocene also exhibited remarkable photothermal stability, as shown in Fig. 6e, with both 40 and 80 μg/mL Pd5‒C showing negligible loss in their maximum temperatures and UV/Vis/NIR spectra (Supplementary Fig. 40) after eight consecutive heating and cooling cycles. The Pd5‒C inverse palladocene even had good photothermal conversion performance under 1064 nm irradiation (0.5 W/cm²), with a temperature elevation of 18.1 °C. However, the photothermal conversion performance of Pd5‒C was relatively poor under 1208 nm irradiation because of the negligible absorption beyond 1100 nm (Fig. 6f; for time-dependent temperature changes, see Supplementary Fig. 41). Referring to the Jablonski energy level diagram (which indicates that a structure with relatively lower PCE might exhibit photoluminescence), we also attempted to investigate the photoluminescence properties of inverse palladocenes under different excitation wavelengths57. Unfortunately, no notable photoluminescence of inverse palladocenes was observed so far, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 42.

Our experiments demonstrated that the outstanding photothermy performance was applicable in multiple fields. One application is laser shielding. Figure 6g‒i show that Pd5‒C (2 mg/mL) effectively reduced 980 nm laser power from 500 to 9 mW, achieving an impressive shielding efficiency of 96.6% (calculated by the equation: R=(I0−I)/I0, where Ib is the permeated laser intensity of blank, I is the permeated laser intensity of the Pd5‒C solution, and I0 is the initial laser intensity). Reducing the concentration to 1.0 mg/mL still yielded a high shielding efficiency of 92.0%, and even for a dilute concentration of 50 μg/mL, the shielding efficiency reached 38.6%. Among the inverse palladocenes, Pd5‒C and Pd5‒O exhibited superior shielding performance for the 980 nm laser, which positively correlated with their PCEs (Fig. 6h and Supplementary Fig. 43a‒d) and conjugation degrees. Pd5‒C even had a good shielding ability for the 1064 nm laser, but performed less efficiently against the 1208 nm laser (Fig. 6i and Supplementary Fig. 43e, f), reflecting its limited absorption beyond 1100 nm.

Another application is for high-temperature degradation. For example, when Pd5‒C was encapsulated in polystyrene and exposed to 980 nm laser irradiation at 0.8 W/cm², it facilitated the degradation of the high ignition temperature polystyrene at ~368 °C (Fig. 6j and Supplementary Fig. 44). In addition, when Pd5‒C was loaded onto a cotton surface, it can ignite the cotton under identical irradiation conditions, suggesting a potential application in ignition (Fig. 6k and Supplementary Movie 1). Furthermore, Pd5‒C also displayed its applicability in temperature/light control, illustrated by the following experiment. When Pd5‒C was encapsulated in polyurethane (30 mg, 1 wt% of Pd5‒C, 0.2 mm thickness) and subjected to continuous 980 nm laser irradiation at 0.4 W/cm², the composite temperature rapidly increased over a stable range of 107.5‒108.5 °C, illustrating precise thermal management capabilities (Fig. 6l). Moreover, the aforementioned Pd5‒C/polyurethane film also exhibited excellent laser shielding performance (Supplementary Fig. 45), achieving a shielding efficiency of 81.8%. Overall, these findings demonstrate the great potential of inverse palladocene materials across a multitude of fields.

## Methods

Materials
Pd(CH3COO)2 (99.9%), polystyrene (PS), and polyurethane (PU) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. 1-Adamantanethiol (Adm-SH, 99%), triphenylphosphine (PPh3), (Ph2P)2CH2 (DPPM), sodium borohydride (NaBH4, 99.8%), triphenylmethanethiol, 2-phenylethanethiol, benzenemethanethiol, cyclohexanethiol, 4-tert-butylphenylthiol, 2,4-dimethylbenzenethiol, toluene, dichloromethane (DCM), tetrahydrofuran (THF), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), and methanol were all purchased from Shanghai Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Pd8‒S nanocluster was prepared according to our previously report15. All chemicals were used as received. The water used in all experiments was ultrapure (resistivity 18.2 MΩ·cm), produced by a Milli-Q NANOpure water system.

Synthesis of Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(S-Adm)6 (denoted as Pd8‒S)15
Pd(CH3COO)2 (50.0 mg, 0.223 mmol) and PPh3 (100.0 mg, 0.381 mmol) were co-dissolved in 8 mL of THF in a three-necked flask with continuous stirring for 5 min, accompanied by a solution color change from yellow to red. Then, a cold water solution containing NaBH4 (100.0 mg, 2.643 mmol) and Adm-SH (150.0 mg, 0.891 mmol) was immediately added all at once under vigorous stirring, accompanied by the solution color turn from red to dark. 25 min later, multi-sized Pd nanoclusters Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z were precipitated out and washed with excess methanol. The Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z nanoclusters were redissolved in toluene (10 mL) and water (5 mL) mixed solution and heated at 80 °C for 24 h. After this two-phase reaction was completed, the black organic solution was washed with methanol for three times. Pd8‒S was isolated from the crude product by preparative thin-layer chromatography (PTLC) in 10.0 mg (yield: 11%, based on the starting material Pd(CH3COO)2). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixture solution of Pd8‒S in DCM/methanol (4:3; 1 mL) for 3 days.

Synthesis of Pd8(PPh)2(PPh3)2(Ph2P=O)(S-Adm)5 (denoted as Pd8‒P)
Pd8‒S (3 mg, 1.16 × 10−3 mmol) and PPh3 (10.0 mg, 0.0381 mmol) were co-dissolved in 2 mL of toluene in a round-bottomed flask with continuous stirring and heated at 80 °C for over 2 weeks under air atmosphere. After the reaction was completed, the black solution was concentrated under reduced pressure to dryness. Pd8‒P was isolated from the crude product of 20 combined reaction batches by preparative thin-layer chromatography (PTLC) in 1.2 mg (yield: 2%, based on the starting material Pd8‒S). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixed solution of Pd8‒P in DCM/methanol (4:3; 1 mL) over 3 days.

Synthesis of Pd6(PPh)(PPh3)(S-Adm)6 (denoted as Pd6)
Pd(CH3COO)2 (50.0 mg, 0.223 mmol) and PPh3 (100.0 mg, 0.381 mmol) were co-dissolved in 8 mL of THF in a three-necked flask with continuous stirring for 5 min, accompanied by a solution color change from yellow to red. Then, a cold water solution containing NaBH4 (100.0 mg, 2.643 mmol) and Adm-SH (150.0 mg, 0.891 mmol) was immediately added all at once under vigorous stirring, accompanied by the solution color turn from red to dark. 10 min later, multi-sized Pd nanoclusters Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z (x, y, and z denote the number of the unit in a nanocluster, and x is larger than z) were precipitated out and washed with excess methanol. The Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z nanoclusters were redissolved in a toluene (10 mL) and water (5 mL) mixed solution and heated at 80 °C for 6 h (This process can turn the muti-sized Pd x(PPh3)y(S-Adm)z nanoclusters to narrowly distributed nanoclusters—size-focusing58. The use of a toluene/water mixed solvent can accelerate the size-focusing, possibly due to some hydrophilic byproducts that can migrate to the water phase, thus promoting the reaction. After this two-phase reaction was completed, the black organic solution was washed with methanol three times. Pd6 was isolated from the crude product by PTLC in 22.4 mg (yield: 30%, based on the starting material Pd(CH3COO)2). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixed solution of Pd6 in DCM/methanol (3:5; 1 mL) for 3 days.

Synthesis of Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2O] (denoted as Pd5‒O)
Pd6 (3 mg, 1.49 × 10−3 mmol) and PPh3 (10.0 mg, 0.0381 mmol) were co-dissolved in 2 mL of toluene in a round-bottomed flask with continuous stirring and heated at 60 °C for over 2 weeks under air atmosphere After the reaction was completed, the black solution was concentrated under reduced pressure to dryness. Pd5‒O was isolated from the crude product of 20 combined reaction batches by PTLC in 1.5 mg (yield: 3%, based on the starting material Pd6). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixture solution of Pd5‒O in DCM/methanol (4:3; 1 mL) over 6 days.

Synthesis of Pd5(PPh)(S-Adm)4[(Ph2P)2CH2] (denoted as Pd5‒C)
Pd(CH3COO)2 (50.0 mg, 0.223 mmol) and DPPM (100.0 mg, 0.260 mmol) were co-dissolved in 8 mL of THF in a three-necked flask with continuous stirring for 5 min, accompanied by a solution color change from yellow to red. Then, a cold water solution containing NaBH4 (100.0 mg, 2.643 mmol) and Adm-SH (150.0 mg, 0.891 mmol) was immediately added all at once under vigorous stirring, accompanied by the solution color turn from red to dark. 30 min later, multi-sized Pd nanoclusters were precipitated out and washed with excess methanol. The precipitate was redissolved in toluene (10 mL) and water (5 mL), mixed solution and heated at 80 °C for 24 h. After this two-phase reaction was completed, the black organic solution was washed with methanol for three times. Pd5‒C was isolated from the crude product by PTLC in 9.8 mg (yield: 13%, based on the starting material Pd(CH3COO)2). Black single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction analysis were obtained by slowly evaporating the mixed solution of Pd5‒C in DCM/methanol (5:4; 1 mL) over 5 days. Pd5‒C nanocluster could also be obtained by the ligand exchange reaction of Pd5‒O (3 mg, 1.77 × 10−3 mmol) and DPPM (10.0 mg, 0.026 mmol) in 2 mL of toluene and heated at 60 °C for 5 h under air atmosphere.

Note that, inverse palladocenes with planar aromatic Pd5 ring unit and unanticipated nonmental-to-metal aromatic Pd5 ring coordination are synthesized under aqueous-, oxygen-containing conditions and demonstrate remarkable stability in air atmosphere, distinctly differing from reported Pd clusters such as cubic Pd8(PAr)6 clusters59, planar Pd7 clusters60 and Pd4 clusters61 (which require strict anhydrous- and oxygen-free conditions for synthesis and most of them are sensitive to air atmosphere).

Construction of Pd nanoclusters/PS and Pd nanoclusters/PU composites
Pd nanoclusters (1 mg) and PS (100 mg) were co-dissolved in 1.5 mL of DCM and dropwise added into quartz grooves. After the volatilization of DCM, pressure was applied to the Pd nanoclusters/PS composites between two quartz sheets, and they were placed under reduced pressure in a vacuum oven for 12 h to fix their shape. To measure the PCE of Pd nanoclusters, the as-prepared Pd nanoclusters/PS films were shaped into 1 cm2 circular discs with a thickness of 0.20‒0.26 mm (detailed calculation procedures are provided in the Photothermal effects and efficiency calculation section of the Supplementary Information). The Pd nanoclusters/PU composites were constructed using a similar process as that for the Pd nanoclusters/PS composites; however, the PU needed to be dissolved in DMF instead of DCM at 90 °C for 12 h.

Characterization
All UV/Vis/NIR absorption spectra were acquired in the wavelength range of 190–1200 nm using a UV-2550 spectrophotometer. Electrospray ionization mass spectra (ESI‒MS) were recorded using a Waters Q-TOF mass spectrometer utilizing a Z-spray source. The sample was first dissolved in toluene (~0.5 g/L) and then diluted (2/1 v/v) with an ethanol solution containing 50 mmol of CsOAc. The sample was directly infused into the chamber at a flow rate of 5 μL/min. The source temperature was maintained at 70 °C, the spray voltage was 2.20 kV, and the cone voltage was adjusted to 60 V. The single crystal X-ray crystallography (SCXC) data of inverse palladocenes were collected using a Bruker D8 VENTURE CMOS PHOTON 100 diffractometer with a Helios MX multilayer monochromator using Ga Kα radiation (λ=1.34139 Å), while the (Ph2P=O) were collected using a XtaLAB Synergy R, HyPix four-circle diffractometer with a mirror monochromator using Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.54184 Å). 1H, 13C, and 31P NMR spectra were recorded with a Bruker Avance-400 spectrometer. The photoluminescence (PL) properties were recorded by a OmniFluo990 LSP using a xenon lamp as the excitation source under liquid nitrogen. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed using a Thermo Scientific K-Alpha XPS spectrometer. Thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA) of Pd nanoclusters (~5 mg) was conducted in a N2 atmosphere (flow rate ~50 mL/min) on a TG/DTA 6300 analyzer (Seiko Instruments, Inc), with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) characterization was carried out on a Hitachi SU8020 under an accelerating voltage of 10 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization was carried out on a Tecnai G2 F20 under the accelerating voltage of 200 kV. Photothermal measurements were conducted using 980 nm (LSR980F-3W-FC), 1064 nm (LSR1064PD-3W-FC), and 1208 nm (LSR1208NL-1.5W-FC) lasers. The temperature was measured using a thermal imager infrared camera (Fotric 227S), with an error range of ±2.0 °C. Real-time temperatures and infrared photos were extracted from the video by FLIR tools software. Laser power was measured by HS1-USB 0516RI24U device with the software of Power Meter-USB. A conventional three-electrode system was used for differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) measurement. The saturated calomel electrode (SCE) (with saturated KCl solution) and carbon rods are used as a reference (RE) and counter electrode (CE), respectively. A Pt disk electrode (1 mm diameter) was used as working electrode (WE). The electrode potentials were controlled by a potentiostat (Zahner, Germen). The inverse palladocenes were dissolved in CH2Cl2/0.1 M Bu4NPF6 of that was constantly purged by N2 (99.99% Nanjing Special Gas Corp.) during the experiments. All electrochemical experiments were carried out at room temperature (ca. 25 °C).

Computational details
The geometry optimizations of the Pd5‒C, Pd5‒O, Pd6, Pd8‒S, and Pd8‒P inverse palladocenes were conducted by using density functional theory (DFT) with the ORCA 4.2.1 package62. The hybrid PBE0 functional and def2-SVP basis sets63,64 were adopted, where all-electron basis sets were used for H, C, P, and S atoms, while relativistic effective core potentials (RECP) with the associated valence basis set were applied for Pd atom. NBO 7.0 package65 was utilized to perform natural population analysis (NPA) and compute natural atomic orbitals (NAOs) for facilitating subsequent adaptive natural density partitioning (AdNDP)66 analyses. AdNDP analysis was calculated with Multiwfn 3.8 package67.

Atomic charge analyses, electron localization functions (ELF)68, and the energy decomposition analysis with natural orbitals for chemical valence (EDA-NOCV)69,70 calculations were performed with Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) functional based on single-point calculations by using ADF 2019.304 package71. The all-electron polarized triple-zeta (TZP) Slater-type basis sets were adopted for Pd atoms, and DZP Slater-type basis sets were adopted for other atoms72. The scalar relativistic (SR) effects were taken into account with the zero-order regular approximation (ZORA)73. Reduced density gradient (RDG)74,75 was calculated with the ORCA 4.2.1 package, in which the RDG curve was visualized by using Multiwfn 3.867 and VMD 1.9.3 software76. The isochemical shielding surfaces (ICSS) analysis was also performed with Multiwfn 3.8 software and visualized by VMD 1.9.3.

The Gibbs free energy calculations at T=298.15 K and P=1 atm were carried out by using PBE77 functional along with LANL2TZ ECP and basis set78,79 for Pd atoms, and all-electron basis set80,81 6–31G* for the rest of atoms. Vibrational frequency calculations were performed to obtain the thermal corrections over the quantum-mechanical energies. Based on the geometries optimized in the gas-phase, single-point calculations were further performed at the higher level of LANL2TZ(f)82 basis set for Pd atoms, and 6–311G*80,81 for the rest of atoms. Dispersion corrections were included in our calculations by employing the D3 version of Grimme’s dispersion with Becke-Johnson damping83. Solvent corrections using the SMD model84 were included by considering the reaction in toluene. All the calculations were performed using the Gaussian 16 package85 unless specified otherwise.

To better reproduce the experimental UV/Vis/NIR absorption spectrum, the simulation was carried out by using the Gaussian 16 package85 with the PBE77 functional for geometry optimization and TD‒DFT calculations. The ECP and basis set LANL2TZ78,79 were used for Pd atoms, and 6–31G* was used for others (H, C, S, and P)80,81. 200 singlet-to-singlet excitation energies were considered in the TD‒DFT calculations. The Kohn‒Sham molecular orbital analysis was performed by using Multiwfn 3.8 program67.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a comprehensive study on the synthesis, characterization, and photothermal properties of a novel
class of Pd-based nanoclusters "inverse palladocenes." The work is highly original and addresses an under-explored area
in organometallic chemistry involving "nonmetal-to-metal" coordination and Pd aromaticity. The inverse palladocenes
demonstrate rigorous structural/electronic characterization and promising applications, particularly in photothermal
conversion and laser shielding.
The study is in general well-organized and the major conclusions are supported by the results, which is suitable for the
audience of Nature Communications. However, there are a few issues should be addressed:
1. In Figure 4f, the RGD plot appears with many jagged edges, making it difficult to fully observe the π-π stacking interaction.
We kindly suggest considering an increase in the number of grid points to improve the visualization.
2. Is there any electron transfer occurring between the phenyl group of the DPPM ligand and the nearby metal five-membered
ring? We kindly suggest calculating the orbital distribution based on the crystal structure to analyze the orbital or
hole-electron distribution within the aggregate. Additionally, it may be helpful to calculate the electrostatic potential of
inverse palladocycles for further analysis.
3. Should the authors provide more details about the testing conditions for the absorption spectra of inverse palladocenes?
For instance, are the samples in the form of powder, thin films, or solutions? If the samples are in solution, it would be
interesting to explore how different polarities of solvents affect their absorption spectra. On the other hand, if the samples are
in the form of powder or thin films, the author could investigate any differences in their absorption spectra under various
conditions.
4. The inverse palladocences synthesized by the author show diverse photothermal conversion capabilities. Referring to the
Jablonski energy level diagram, might a structure with relatively lower photothermal conversion efficiency exhibit
photoluminescence? If this material features near-infrared luminescence properties, its potential application could be greatly
broadened.
5. The author noted that the photothermal conversion originates from the conjugation of the five-membered palladium
aromatic ring of inverse palladocences. However, we also observe five-membered palladium aromatic rings in Pd8 and Pd6.
Why Pd8 and Pd6 don't demonstrate sufficiently strong photothermal conversion capabilities?
6. In the final paragraph of the article, the author mentions that Pd5-C encapsulated in polystyrene assist in the degradation
of polystyrene at 368 °C. However, in supplementary figure 25, the Pd5-C decomposed at ~300 °C and reached a mass loss
of 60% by ~50 °C. Considering this information, why the reaction might specifically occur at 368 °C?
7. It is suggested to present the values involved in the PCE calculation in a table format for better clarity and organization.
8. In which solution was the photothermal conversion tested (Figure 6a), water or toluene?

Metallocenes with layered structures have had a significant impact on the development
of organometallic chemistry. In particular, metallocenes with high catalytic activity and
electrochemical redox ability play a very important role in their applications. This paper
proposes a new group of compounds called “Inverse palladocenes”, which are different
from the general “palladocenes”, which are metallocenes based on palladium. These
groups of materials have a high degree of novelty in the fields of metal organic
chemistry and cluster chemistry. Furthermore, these researches have already been

Question 1: What is the essential difference between Reference 15 (Angew. Chem. Int.
Ed. 63, e202313491 (2024).) and this study?
Response: Thank the reviewer for the question. We did synthesize the
Pd (PPh) (PPh ) (S-Adm) (Pd –S for short) nanocluster previously (Angew. Chem. Int.
8 2 3 2 6 8
Ed. 63, e202313491 (2024)), which might indicate the emergence of a novel type of
material: inverse metallocene. However, we didn’t propose the concept “inverse
metallocene” in that work since additional instances are required to validate a single
case report. In particular, at that time it remained uncertain whether metal five-
membered ring structures analogous to the cyclopentadienyl anion (Cp) structure exist.
Here we proposed the concept “inverse metallocene” and demonstrate that the five-
membered aromatic metal ring is a fundamental metal building block for inverse
metallocene by developing synthesis methods and synthesizing a series of new
compounds. Therefore, one point of this work is that it declares the birth of a novel type
of materials with fundamental study values and great application potentials. There are
some other essential differences between the two works as summarized below:
i) the longest laser irradiation wavelength was extended from the previous 808 nm
to 1208 nm, which is nontrivial for practical applications, and the high
photothermal conversion efficiency (PCE) of 14.7% per metal atom was
achieved in this work, which considerably outperforms that for Pd ‒S and other
8
reported materials as displayed in Fig. 6c and supplementary Table 9;
22
ii) a novel physical quantity—nominal coplanar bond length standard deviation
(S ) was introduced to evaluate the conjugation degree of inverse palladocenes
ncp
and the conjugation-correlated photothermy was revealed in this work; it is also
found that the NIR absorption peak position and intensity positively correlate
with conjugation degree for the series of inverse palladocenes;
iii) the application of photothermy was greatly extended to a large range of fields
including laser shielding, high-temperature degradation, ignition and
temperature control in this work, demonstrating great potentials of inverse
palladocenes for practical applications;
iv) the nonmetal-aromatic ring to metallo-aromatic-ring weak interaction was
found in the crystal structure of Pd ‒C, which was not previously reported;
5
...
In short, we have made great advances in the synthesis, structure, property and
structure-property correlation study of a novel type of materials, and we have further
expanded the application fields of this type of materials. Therefore, this work is
essentially different from the previous work, and its novelty, significance and impact
are nontrivial.
